per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid’s Orthotics & Prosthetics policy does **not** cover certain items even if they relate to orthotic or prosthetic needs. In general, coverage requires that the item be medically necessary, ordered by an authorized clinician, appropriate for the beneficiary’s condition and functional needs, and not primarily for convenience. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

## Specifically not covered under Policy 5B

The policy’s “Specific Criteria Not Covered by Medicaid” lists these categories as not covered:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience** or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup or duplicate devices** kept on hand or available in different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care** [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

The policy also generally requires that a covered item **not be furnished primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider**, which reinforces the convenience exclusion. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

Under the general coverage criteria, the procedure, product, or service must be:

- **Individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis**
- **Not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**
- Able to be **safely furnished**
- Not replaced by an **equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment** available statewide
- Furnished in a manner **not primarily intended for convenience** of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

## Additional specific coverage criteria for orthotics/prosthetics

The policy also says orthotic and prosthetic items must:

- Be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- Be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level
- Be **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place
- Be supported by a **face-to-face encounter** with the ordering clinician no more than **6 months** before initiation
- Have the beneficiary’s need **reviewed at least annually** [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

The policy further explains:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary as a replacement for **all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary must need the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes** [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

## Practical bottom line

A DME-type item under this policy will generally be covered only if it is truly an **orthotic or prosthetic device**, is **medically necessary**, **clinically appropriate**, and **not duplicative, convenience-based, or payable by another source**. Items for comfort, backup use, nursing-facility residents, hospice, or another agency’s responsibility are specifically excluded. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

I checked amendments for Policy 5B and did not find any listed amendments; the authoritative document returned was the current **Orthotics & Prosthetics** policy.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services, the policy does set specific **entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria**. In the medical record, the provider must document all three. This comes from the current version of **[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)**, effective **April 15, 2025**. I also checked amendments, and the cited 8C document is the authoritative current document.

## Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets the **entrance criteria** if all of the following are present:

- A current **DSM-5** diagnosis;
- Behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment consistent with and associated with that diagnosis;
- If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary refuses it, outpatient services may be provided until that higher level is available or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care;
- The beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions; and
- There is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective under North Carolina community practice standards.  
  Source: **§ 3.2.1.1** of **[8C](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)**.

## Continued service criteria
To continue services, the policy requires:

### First, at least one of these:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not** been restored, improved, or sustained within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary remains at risk for **relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- Functional gains are **tenuous**.

### And, in addition, at least one of these:
- Current treatment plan goals have been achieved, but **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; or
- The beneficiary is making **satisfactory progress** toward goals and there is documentation supporting that.  
  Source: **§ 3.2.1.2** of **[8C](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)**.

## Discharge criteria
A beneficiary meets the **discharge criteria** if any one of the following applies:

- The beneficiary’s level of functioning has improved with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; or
- The beneficiary has not improved despite modifications to the treatment plan and needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality under North Carolina community practice standards.  
  Source: **§ 3.2.1.3** of **[8C](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)**.

## Documentation requirement
The provider record must include:
- an individualized treatment plan; and
- documentation of the **entrance criteria, continued service criteria, and discharge criteria**.  
Source: **§ 7.3.1** of **[8C](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)**.

If you want, I can also turn this into a short advocacy-friendly checklist for chart review or medical-necessity appeals.

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries under 21, the EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a condition, but it does **not** waive prior approval requirements. Ordering practitioners for these services are limited to specific listed practitioner types. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current per amendment check)

## EPSDT effect on outpatient therapy coverage

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A includes an **EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age** in § 2.2.1. That section cites **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [Social Security Act § 1905(r)]** and indicates the usual limits do not extend to services that are:
- unsafe,
- ineffective,
- experimental or investigational, or
- not medical in nature / not generally recognized as accepted medical practice.  
([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current per amendment check)

For outpatient therapy specifically, Policy 10A also sets pediatric visit guidelines in § 5.4. For speech-language and audiology therapy, visits for beneficiaries under 21 are tied to medical necessity and severity of deficit, with:
- mild impairment: **6 to 26** visits,
- moderate impairment: **up to 46** visits,
- severe impairment: **up to 52** visits,  
and the authorization period cannot exceed **six calendar months**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 5.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current per amendment check)

So, in practical terms: **EPSDT may allow medically necessary outpatient therapy for a beneficiary under 21 even when ordinary policy limitations would otherwise restrict coverage, but only if the service is medically necessary and not excluded for the reasons listed above.**

## Prior approval under EPSDT

Policy 10A is explicit that EPSDT does **not** remove prior approval requirements:

> “If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.”  
([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current per amendment check)

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

Policy 10A § 3.1.2 lists the authorized ordering practitioners for outpatient specialized therapies. The ordering practitioner may be a:
- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP)  
([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 3.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current per amendment check)

I did **not** find a separate, stricter ordering-practitioner list in the sections retrieved for beneficiaries under 21. Based on the text I could verify, the policy’s general ordering-practitioner list applies.

## Bottom line

For a Medicaid beneficiary under 21 seeking outpatient therapy:
1. **EPSDT can support coverage beyond normal policy limits** when the therapy is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s condition.
2. **EPSDT does not eliminate prior approval** when the service otherwise requires it.
3. The service must still be ordered by one of the practitioner types listed in § 3.1.2: **MD, DO, DPM, CNM, PA, or NP**.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — **NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for a beneficiary who lives in an assisted living facility**, but only if the person meets the congregate-setting PCS eligibility criteria.

Under Clinical Coverage Policy **3L-1**, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who **resides in a congregate facility licensed by North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)** or certain licensed group homes, and who also meets the required functional and medical criteria. An assisted living facility generally falls within the adult care home/congregate-setting framework addressed by this policy. See **§ 3.2.1** of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

Coverage is **not automatic** just because the person lives in assisted living. PCS is not covered if, for example, the beneficiary does not complete the required independent assessment, receives services outside the primary congregate living setting, exceeds the approved amount, or has family/informal caregivers who are willing, able, and available to meet the need. See **§ 4.2** and **§ 4.1** of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## Bottom line
- **Yes, potentially covered** in an assisted living/adult care home setting.
- **Only if** the beneficiary meets the policy’s medical, functional, and setting requirements.
- **Not covered** if the beneficiary fails the additional non-covered criteria in the policy.

I checked for amendments to Policy **3L-1** and did not find any change notices superseding it in the corpus, so [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment) is the current authoritative document I can confirm here.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—HCWD policy does **not set a maximum earned-income limit**. The policy says HCWD covers individuals **“regardless of total countable income”** after the Phase III revision, but it **does keep a 150% FPL cap on unearned income**. In other words, the income cap the policy identifies is on **unearned income**, not earned income. [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf); [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

## Governing HCWD income rule
To qualify, a person must meet the HCWD income requirements, and the current MA-2180 text states:

- People with **unearned income greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible for HCWD**.
- People whose **total countable income is at or below 150% of FPL** have **no cost sharing** other than applicable copayments.
- People whose **total countable income is greater than 150% of FPL** must pay a **$50 annual enrollment fee**.
- People whose **total countable monthly income exceeds 200% of FPL** must also pay a **monthly premium** in addition to the enrollment fee.
- The monthly premium increases by income range until income **exceeds 450% of FPL**, at which point a **full premium** is due. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

The 2014 change notice specifically says MA-2180 was revised to **“remove limits on countable income except for the 150% of Federal Poverty Level (FPL) cap on unearned income”** and to provide sliding-scale premiums. [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

## Premiums that apply
The surfaced MA-2180 premium chart provides these monthly premium amounts:

- **0–150% FPL:** $0
- **151–200% FPL:** $0
- **201–250% FPL:** **$196 individual / $265 couple**
- **251–300% FPL:** **$235 individual / $318 couple**
- **301–350% FPL:** **$274 individual / $370 couple**
- **351–400% FPL:** **$313 individual / $423 couple**
- **401–450% FPL:** **$352 individual / $476 couple**
- **451% FPL and above:** **$875 individual / $875 couple** [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

Also, the manual includes the note: **“Refer to Job Aid: Forced Eligibility to process HCWD premium.”** [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

## Important amendment note
MA-2180 has been amended, and the amendment history shows that **the HCWD premiums income chart was updated by 2025 change notice**: [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf). So while the **premium structure** above is clearly supported by the current surfaced MA-2180 text, I **could not verify the current 2025 dollar income-range cutoffs** from the surfaced evidence alone. The cited chart supports the listed **premium amounts**, but the exact FPL-to-dollar conversion ranges may have been updated by that 2025 amendment.

## Bottom line
- **Maximum earned income limit?** **No, not as a stated HCWD eligibility cap.**
- **Unearned income limit?** **Yes — unearned income over 150% FPL makes the person ineligible.**
- **Premiums?**  
  - **$0** through **200% FPL**  
  - **$50 annual enrollment fee** once income is **over 150% FPL**  
  - **Monthly premium starts above 200% FPL** and rises by bracket, up to **$875** at **451% FPL and above**. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

If you want, I can also give you a **plain-English HCWD fee/premium summary for advocates**, or help figure out **whether a specific person’s earned vs. unearned income would trigger the fee or premium**.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a Medicaid-eligible nursing facility resident, with **no more than 15 consecutive days unless NC Medicaid approves more**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]

## Conditions that must be met

Therapeutic leave is allowed only if:

- the person is a **Medicaid-eligible resident** occupying a nursing facility bed that Medicaid is paying for;
- the leave is **for therapeutic purposes only**;
- the leave is **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**;
- the **need for leave is documented in the resident’s plan of care**; and

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
If a **Private Duty Nursing (PDN) provider** terminates services, the provider’s main NC Medicaid notification duty is to notify **NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, using the required discharge form and, in some situations, extra supporting information.

## NC Medicaid policy requirements

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** in **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**, which appears current based on amendment review:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  the provider **must submit the DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form) to NC Medicaid within five (5) business days**.

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary because there is another source of nursing care coverage:**  
  the provider must **notify NC Medicaid and submit the DMA-3513 within five (5) business days**.  
  That notification must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided** and can be billed to Medicaid, and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary:**  
  the PDN provider must provide **to NC Medicaid within five (5) business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order to terminate PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)**.

- If services end because the beneficiary **loses NC Medicaid eligibility**, or **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason, including hospitalization, then **the prior approval process must be started again** under Sections 5.1 and 5.2.  
  Also, the policy says that a discharge decision by the attending physician and/or PDN provider **cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid**.  
  Citation: **Section 5.2.4.1** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**.

## If the termination is by NC Medicaid or a managed care plan

That is different from a provider’s own discharge. If **NC Medicaid or a managed care plan** terminates, suspends, or reduces previously authorized Medicaid-covered services, written notice with appeal information is required.

Under **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**, which also appears current based on amendment review:

- An **MCO, PIHP, or PAHP** must give the enrollee **timely and adequate written notice** of an adverse benefit determination.  
- The notice must explain:
  - what action was taken,
  - the reasons,
  - appeal rights,
  - how to appeal,
  - expedited appeal rights, and
  - continuation-of-benefits rights where applicable.  
  Citation: **42 CFR § 438.404** in **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**.

- Required notices to enrollees must be provided in a manner that is **easily understood and readily accessible**, including translation/alternative-format rules for termination notices.  
  Citation: **42 CFR § 438.10** in **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**.

## Bottom line

For a **PDN provider-initiated termination**, the clearest rule is:

- **Notify NC Medicaid within 5 business days**
- **Submit DMA-3513**
- Include any required extra information:
  - **last billable service date**
  - **other coverage source**, if applicable
  - **physician termination order**, if the physician discharged the beneficiary

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** means the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and plan-of-care rules. Those services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis,
- **Home health aide services**,
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in normal living settings, and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology/audiology services** as an optional home health benefit category.  
Cited authority: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440) § 440.70. The document is current based on the retrieved federal authority, and no amendments were returned by the amendment check.

## Governing federal rule

Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(a)**, home health services are services that are provided to a beneficiary:

1. **At the person’s place of residence**;
2. **On written orders** of a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant working in accordance with state law, as part of a **written plan of care**; and
3. For nursing, aide, and therapy-related services covered under § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4), the ordering practitioner must **review the written plan of care every 60 days**.  
For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances under § 440.70(b)(3), the regulation uses a separate ordering and review framework, including review of need by a physician or other licensed practitioner at least annually, with further review frequency determined case by case.  
Cited authority: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440) § 440.70(a), (b)(3).

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided at the beneficiary’s **“place of residence.”** But the regulation also makes clear what **does not** count as a place of residence for this purpose.

### Excluded settings
Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(c)**, a beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

with a limited exception for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide.  
Cited authority: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440) § 440.70(c).

### Broader place-of-residence rule
The regulation further states that nothing in § 440.70 should be read to prohibit a beneficiary from receiving home health services in **any setting in which normal life activities take place**, other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**.  
It also explicitly states that home health services **cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**.  
Cited authority: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440) § 440.70(c)(1).

## Supporting context

Federal Medicaid also separately recognizes some home- and community-based services in other provisions, but those do **not change the core definition of “home health services” in § 440.70**. For your question, **§ 440.70 is the controlling definition and location rule**.  
Cited authority: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440) § 440.70; see also § 440.182.

## Bottom line

Federal law defines Medicaid **home health services** as certain nursing, aide, supply/equipment, and therapy services furnished under required practitioner orders and a written plan of care, and they must be provided at the beneficiary’s **place of residence**. They may be provided in **settings where normal life activities occur**, but **not** in a **hospital, nursing facility, ICF/IID**, or another setting where Medicaid pays or could pay for **inpatient room-and-board services**. They also **cannot be restricted only to people who are homebound**.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice, **“terminally ill” means the beneficiary has a life expectancy of six months or less**. The hospice certification materials must support that terminal diagnosis with individualized clinical information. In later benefit periods, the narrative must explain why the face-to-face clinical findings support **a life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.1; D. *Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness*.

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**, and the hospice provider must obtain it **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within two calendar days after the period begins, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two days, with the written certification completed before billing. Initial certifications may be completed no more than **15 calendar days before the effective date of election**, and recertifications no more than **15 calendar days before the next benefit period**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) § 5.4.1 (effective Mar. 15, 2024; current per amendment check).

## Who must sign it

For the **initial 90-day period**, the hospice must obtain a written certification from:

- **the hospice medical director or the physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
- **the individual’s attending physician, if the individual has one**.

For **subsequent periods**, only the **hospice medical director or physician member of the IDG** must certify. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) § 5.4.3.

## What the certification must contain

The certification or recertification must include:

- a physician narrative that briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis and attests that the physician personally composed the narrative after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- a narrative reflecting the beneficiary’s **individual clinical circumstances**;
- the **election period dates** to which the certification applies; and
- the certifying physician’s **signature and date**.

For the **third benefit period recertification and every recertification after that**, a **face-to-face encounter** by a hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner must occur **before**, but no more than **30 calendar days before**, the recertification, to gather clinical findings on continued eligibility; and the narrative must explain why those findings support a life expectancy of six months or less. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) § 5.4.1; D. *Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness*.

## Bottom line

NC Medicaid hospice eligibility requires a physician-certified prognosis of **six months or less to live if the illness runs its normal course**, documented through a written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period, with specific timing, signatory, and narrative requirements under Policy 3D.

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Speech therapy **can be provided by telehealth under NC Medicaid only for a limited set of speech/language evaluation and treatment services, and only when the telehealth use meets specific beneficiary-centered conditions**. In particular:

- Telehealth may be medically necessary when the beneficiary’s condition means **exposure to others should be avoided**, or when the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** with limited access to qualified providers.
- **Unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable, telehealth must be an adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement.**
- Telehealth must be used **in the beneficiary’s best interest**, **not for therapist convenience**.
- Telehealth **cannot be used solely to increase therapist productivity**.  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective Feb. 1, 2025, section “e. Telehealth”)

## Which speech-language services are telehealth-eligible

NC Medicaid’s speech/language tables indicate that the following are telehealth-eligible:

### Evaluation codes
- **92521** — Yes
- **92522** — Yes
- **92523** — Yes
- **92524** — Yes
- **92607** — Yes
- **92608** — Yes

Not telehealth-eligible in that table:
- **92551**
- **92610**
- **92612**
- **92626**
- **92627**
- **96125**  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “Speech/Language Evaluation”)

### Treatment codes
- **92507** — Yes
- **92526** — **Yes (oral motor only)**
- **92609** — Yes

Not telehealth-eligible in that table:
- **92508**
- **92630**
- **92633**  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “Speech/Language Treatment”)

## Other ordinary speech-therapy rules still apply

Telehealth does **not** eliminate the usual medical-necessity standards for speech-language therapy. The policy’s speech-language therapy section still requires medically necessary treatment and documentation consistent with the beneficiary’s condition. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3)

## Bottom line

A speech therapy service may be delivered by telehealth under NC Medicaid **only if**:

1. the specific speech/language service is listed as **telehealth eligible** in Policy 10A;  
2. telehealth is **medically necessary** for the beneficiary, such as to avoid exposure or because access is limited in a remote/underserved area;  
3. telehealth is used **as a supplement to in-person care**, unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable; and  
4. it is **for the beneficiary’s benefit**, not therapist convenience or productivity.  

I checked amendments for Policy 10A and the retrieved results identify **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, effective Feb. 1, 2025, as the current authoritative document**.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care plans do **not automatically have to meet a federally imposed minimum MLR unless the state elects to require one**. But every state **must** require each Medicaid MCO, PIHP, and PAHP to **calculate and report** its MLR. If a state chooses to impose a minimum MLR, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## Federal rule

### 1) Calculation and reporting are mandatory
For contracts starting on or after July 1, 2017, the state must ensure through its contracts that each Medicaid MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR in accordance with the federal rule. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 2) Minimum threshold is conditional
Federal law says: **if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85%**. So the federal floor for any state-imposed minimum is 85%, but the regulation itself does **not** say every Medicaid managed care organization nationwide must always meet 85% absent state adoption of a minimum. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 3) Oversight and remittances
If a state uses a minimum MLR requirement, the state must annually submit to CMS a summary of each plan’s MLR reporting, including the numerator, denominator, MLR percentage, member months, and any remittances owed. If the state requires remittances for failure to meet the minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the federal share and separately report the remittance methodology. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina’s available implementation evidence here is from **SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care**, which the amendment check returned as current in this corpus. In section 3.3, NC states that its rates are designed to reasonably achieve a medical loss ratio, and it further addresses the situation where an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP owes a **remittance** for failing to meet the **minimum MLR required by the State**. In that event, NC says it will reimburse CMS for the federal share and submit the required separate methodology report with its annual submission. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** plans must **calculate and report** MLR; any **state-chosen minimum** must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **NC implementation shown in the retrieved materials:** NC recognizes the federal remittance/reporting framework and states that if a remittance is owed for failure to meet the state’s minimum MLR, NC will handle the federal-share repayment and reporting to CMS. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

One caution: the NC section retrieved here is abbreviated and does **not fully show** whether NC’s own operative managed care contracts or other state materials expressly set the minimum MLR at a specific percentage in this corpus excerpt. What I can verify from the text retrieved is the **federal minimum floor of 85% if NC imposes a minimum**, and NC’s acknowledgment of the remittance/reporting mechanism.

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the policy’s general medical-necessity standards **and** the therapy meets the policy’s CAR-T-specific requirements. Under current Clinical Coverage Policy **11A-17**, the specific CAR-T coverage criteria are:

- **The CAR-T therapy must be approved by the U.S. FDA.**
- **It must be administered in accordance with the FDA-approved guidelines**, including:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions.
- **It must be administered at a certified or authorized treatment center.**
- **If the therapy is subject to an FDA-required REMS program**, the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS, and providers must be trained to manage:
  - cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and
  - neurological toxicities.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.2.1, effective 4/1/2025.

In addition, the policy’s **general coverage criteria** require that the service be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis,
- safely furnished, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide, and
- furnished in a way not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1, effective 4/1/2025.

## When NC Medicaid does not cover CAR-T therapy
The policy also identifies situations where CAR-T is **not covered**, including when:

- the therapy is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is administered **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy that requires REMS is given at a facility **not enrolled in that REMS**;
- the beneficiary is receiving a **repeat CAR-T treatment after having previously received another CAR-T therapy**;
- the beneficiary’s psychosocial history limits the ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker noncompliance makes adherence to the medical regimen improbable.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.2.1, effective 4/1/2025.

The policy also says CAR-T is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet eligibility requirements, does not meet the Section 3 criteria, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.  
[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.1, effective 4/1/2025.

## Prior approval documentation
If you also need the **documents NC Medicaid requires for prior approval**, the policy lists items such as:

- a signed letter of medical necessity,
- documentation of past chemotherapy regimens and dates,
- clinical and social history,
- verification that the administering facility is a qualified/certified/authorized treatment center,
- recent HIV and hepatitis serologies,
- diagnostic and procedure results including bone marrow biopsy,
- and a complete psychological/social evaluation addressing compliance, support network, post-treatment care plan, and relevant mental health/substance use/legal history.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2, effective 4/1/2025.

I checked amendment status for Policy 11A-17, and the retrieved authority indicates the **current authoritative document is the 4/1/2025 version**. If you want, I can also turn this into a **checklist for prior authorization submissions**.

per_question.question: Until what age should physicians provide fluoride varnish applications for Medicaid beneficiaries, and what oral screening requirements apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
Physicians should provide Medicaid-covered fluoride varnish **from tooth eruption until the beneficiary reaches 3½ years of age**. The service is also **limited to beneficiaries under 3½ years of age**, **allowed once every 60 calendar days**, and **limited to six applications before age 3½**. [[Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment), effective Dec. 4, 2019, § 5.3]

## Oral screening requirements

The required oral screening elements are:

- **Early caries screening** and detection of notable findings, including obvious pathology of hard and soft tissues in the oral cavity, **using a dental mirror and directed light**;
- **Counseling and educational materials** on good oral hygiene practices and nutrition for children;
- **Prescribing a fluoride supplement, if indicated**, consistent with the guidelines of the American Academy of Pediatrics; and
- **Application of fluoride varnish to all erupted primary teeth**, beginning at tooth eruption until age 3½. [[Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment), effective Dec. 4, 2019, § 7.2]

## Required documentation

The beneficiary’s health record must document:

- the **oral evaluation** and any notable findings;
- **preventive oral health and dietary counseling** with the primary caregiver;
- **application of fluoride varnish**; and
- **referral to a dentist, if appropriate**. [[Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment), effective Dec. 4, 2019, § 7.2]

I checked amendments for this policy and the tool returned **no amendments**, with **Physician Fluoride Varnish Services (Policy 1A-23)** as the authoritative current document.

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than the participant’s individual base budget if the participant believes their needs cannot be met within that budget. Under the policy, the SIS results and base budget are “guidelines” and “do not constitute a binding limit” on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized. If the LME/MCO determines the services are medically necessary, they must be authorized even if they exceed the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective Nov. 1, 2016; amendment check returned no later amending notice in the corpus).

## If the participant believes the budget is not enough

The policy says the participant:

- **may request services in excess of the base budget** if their needs cannot be met within it;
- is not limited by the base budget as an absolute cap, because the budget is a **guideline, not a binding limit**; and
- can have those services authorized if the **LME/MCO finds them medically necessary**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## If the request is denied

If authorization for requested services is denied, the LME/MCO must notify the individual:

- of the **reasons for the decision**; and
- **how to appeal**.  

The policy also references **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget** if the individual wants to do so. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## What the policy suggests happens next when needs are very high

For very intensive service needs, the policy contemplates continued authorization based on **medical necessity review**, and says the treatment team should meet to review the person’s status and identify sustainable supports. That review should consider options:

- **within the Innovations Waiver**, and
- **outside the waiver**, such as **Medicaid State Plan Services**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

The base budget is **not an absolute ceiling**. A participant can ask for more, and if the extra services are **medically necessary**, NC Innovations policy says they can be authorized despite the budget. If the request is denied, the participant must be told why and how to appeal, and may also pursue a grievance about the base budget.
